title: Startups Should Evaluate Engineers Differently From Big Companies
author: Greg Ojesterson
summary: Ojesterson argues that engineering evaluation frameworks designed for large companies fundamentally fail in startup environments where different skills and mindsets are required. Startups need to evaluate based on speed of learning, ability to work with ambiguity, ownership mindset, and pragmatism—not the deep specialization and process adherence valued at scale. Young engineers excel at big companies through established systems; startup success requires different qualities entirely. Misapplying big-company evaluation to startup hires leads to poor fits and missed talent opportunities.
points: Startup engineering evaluation should prioritize learning velocity and ambiguity tolerance over specialization.
Big-company evaluation frameworks reward depth in stable systems; startups need breadth and pragmatism.
The best big-company engineers often underperform in startups if they lack ownership mentality.
Startup hiring should emphasize learning agility and ability to work without complete information.
Using big-company evaluation criteria in startups leads to hiring mismatches and retention issues.
Different environments require different evaluation criteria—this is often overlooked.
quotes: The engineer who excels at a large company through mastery of established systems may struggle in startup chaos.
Startups need engineers who are comfortable learning fast and shipping imperfectly.
The ability to work with ambiguity and incomplete information matters more in startups than depth.
Big-company engineers often fail in startups because they expect the systems and clarity that don't exist.
Startup evaluation should focus on ownership mentality, not just technical depth.
The best startup engineers are those who thrive in learning and building rather than optimizing.
Specialization is a liability in early-stage startups where adaptability is essential.
Startups need people who can move fast with incomplete information and learn on the job.
The evaluation criteria you use will either attract or repel the right startup engineers.
